*Part VI · Where we stand*

# 18. What is built today

*One compact chapter about today, November 2026, read from the status page of Trustwork's public repository. Every other chapter of this book tells the system as it will be; this one says what exists, in the engine's own five words, and what does not. The repository's status page is authoritative and changes whenever a work package is accepted; this chapter is its shape at the date of the edition.*

## Five words

**[Live]** means implemented end to end on PostgreSQL with automated tests, including negative authorisation tests, and not yet deployed to production anywhere. **[Demo]** means the interface exists and is tested in a browser on synthetic data; nothing is stored, and buttons that would act externally are imitations that say so. **[Contract]** means the data shapes, state machines and invariants are frozen as tested schemas, with no storage or API yet. **[Designed]** means an accepted design document or decision record describes it and no code exists. **[Proposed]** means the handbook designs it for the first time, with work packages, and it is open for review. Where this book describes something the repository has not yet designed at all, it says so: "a direction of this book" is not a status word.

## Live, in the API and not deployed **[Live]**

Accounts and sign-in: registration with e-mail verification, where mail leaves through the outbox and the worker with a provider-neutral adapter that no deployment yet points at a mail server, so the default transport records messages instead of sending them; login, recovery, step-up, sessions, two-step verification with an authenticator app, Google and Apple linking through a fake provider. People and companies: public reads, memberships with one active employer, profiles public only with recorded, versioned and revocable consent, company claims (in review) with disputes decided by two reviewers and takeover protection, verification recipes, and public-register facts from adapters that run as deterministic fakes and go live only with a second person. Projects: plans with versions from draft to approved to superseded, taxonomy-keyed items, plan changes with timing facts, per-item sharing with invited parties, permit records, the diary and the site location; plan items that become task requests with immutable, digest-bound offers, or consultation requests with frozen proposals showing the full price and the hub's commission.

Publishing: publications with immutable versions and a computed digest, corrections as new versions with a visible note, retractions that keep their explanation, sources, review by a second editor, feeds. The magazine: numbered, dated issues per hub frozen at release. Buying and selling: catalogue offerings, needs, requests for quotes with immutable versions, quote versions, comparison, negotiation, agreements, acceptance with consent, orders and order changes. Procurement: approval routes with built-in separation of duties and never approval by silence, and a company's private supplier base that nothing leaks from. Execution and reputation: claims, evidence, human-only counterparty decisions, defects and remediation, disputes with an appeal to a different reviewer, reviews with responses, fair timing from recorded plan changes, explainable reputation snapshots with method version, samples and exclusions and no public score, and the builder's tools: credentials checked through a fake register, portfolio, relationship-bound confirmations, contributions, timeliness, limitations with appeals.

The agent: durable mandates confirmed only on the first-party form with step-up, inert chat proposals, one mandate store behind every agent check, runs whose money actions reserve a budget and persist the attempt before dispatch, fake order, payment and channel providers, reconciliation of unknown outcomes, goals, agent-to-agent envelopes, negotiation sessions with round limits, the company's one representative with an accountable person, the module registry, the hub agent policy with second-person activation, the runtime and the adapter for an outside AI chat, with no model and no live provider connected; agent usage prices, metering, quotas, plans and prepaid lots (in review); the authorisation server for outside connections; and a deterministic agent-safety suite against a fully hijacked scripted model, part of the test run. Communications: context threads per work object with no generic inbox, notifications, versioned templates activated in every hub language by a second person. Billing: neutral offers, entitlements, two budget kinds, reservations and a balanced ledger; fee governance and public pricing; the payment port with a deterministic fake, an idempotent webhook inbox and reconciliation, in review, with every acceptance item tied to its test, a review checklist against held funds, and no licensed provider connected. Privacy operations, in part: a person's own requests and preferences, exports, marketing objections, source corrections and audited holds. Country packs for Uzbekistan, Georgia, Armenia, Azerbaijan, the United States and the United Kingdom, partial packs for Canada and Mexico, a European Union layer, and restricted places refused at every entry point.

Hubs: territories, versioned configuration with second-person activation, launch gates, legal document versions with counsel approvals, provider keys with a default-deny egress matrix and spending caps, and the setup wizard, whose backend and first run are complete. Platform administration: scoped staff roles with separation of duties, elevated sessions, second-person approvals bound to an action digest, case access grants and no impersonation, moderation, appeals, support without "log in as user", a pipeline engine, and local data mining with legal basis and retention. The staff lifecycle of a hub (in review): a staff directory and each person's effective access, staff invitations by e-mail with a second person for sensitive roles, eligible roles activated just in time, access-review campaigns that never remove anyone silently, and the function accountability of the hub operating company, so that who answers for each function is recorded, suspended when the holder loses the role and handed over through a guided offboarding. Federation: node identity, signed manifests and double-opt-in peering, in review, with nothing else of the mesh protocol implemented yet. Sanctions compliance: the jurisdiction gate at the proxy and the API, baseline lists ingested in file and fake modes, the screening engine with review cases and appeals, re-screening on every list version, and gates on quotes, acceptance, orders and payouts. Files through an object-storage port with quarantine. A background worker with durable jobs and dead letters. A design system of accessible components with the brand mark.

And the web application runs on this API. With demo mode off, which is the default, sign-up with e-mail verification, sign-in and sign-out, recovery, step-up, sessions and password change, company creation and inviting colleagues, accepting an invitation from the mailed link, and creating and publishing projects work in the browser; the public company, people and project pages show only what the API serves; the terms and privacy pages show the hub's active legal texts or say plainly that none is in force; procurement and sales, the notifications page, news, articles, the magazine and the workspace publication lists read the live API; and the feeds use the same public projections. A browser suite runs these flows against a real API and database. Of the hub console, the setup wizard runs on the live API, and in live mode the console reads the API for the viewer, the node and the hubs, and sends approval decisions, the hub's identity, modes and module switches, a data residency change, legal drafts and launch-gate checks to it; the staff screen with invitations is in progress. Screens not yet connected to an API, events, the academy and the assistant, show their empty states.

## Demo, on synthetic data **[Demo]**

The whole public site and workspace in seven languages, English the reference and the others machine drafts awaiting native review, Spanish included: with the United States as default country it shows the San Diego demo hub, otherwise the original Uzbekistan example. Login, sign-up and onboarding screens; directories, profiles, company pages; project pages; news, articles and weekly magazine issues; events with list, page, registration, ticket, a demo payment labelled as moving no money, and a calendar file; courses and certificates on a person's page with a public certificate check; partner directories with filters; the assistant page with mandates, approvals and runs from demo data; and the remaining sections of the hub console on fixtures, where simulated decisions are never real approvals. A release candidate on a full local container stack with demo mode off has proved sign-up with mail over real SMTP to a sink, company creation, an invitation and a project published to the public site, on synthetic data, with nothing deployed.

## Contract and Designed **[Contract]**

Frozen as tested schemas: person, session and auth commands; membership, claims and legal identifiers from country packs; ownership and milestones; publication, version and corrections; delivery claims, acceptance records and assertions; mandate, approval, action states and reconciliation, with the capability registry; the mesh protocol with conformance vectors; the hub console contract; the pack schema; the jurisdiction gate, screening and attestation contracts; retrieval generations and citations. Designed and not coded: Microsoft and generic sign-in providers, the staff console for disputes and appeals, governed hybrid retrieval with a vector extension, payment and other provider adapters per package, the admin surface of the connection server. The plan editor in the workspace and the function catalogue with team presets of the hub operating company are open work packages.

## Proposed **[Proposed]**

Organiser tools, check-in and payouts for events; course authoring, assessments and accreditation per hub; the needs board, explainable matching and introductions; the procurement and supply suite and the supplier bid desk; manufacturer and supplier knowledge on plan steps; the portable reputation passport; syndication, cross-node deals and federated sign-in; the remaining hub console screens on the live API; the public hub directory, designed to be run by Contribuda (to be confirmed); paid consultations; identity wallets, e-signatures, open BIM exchange, an installable offline-first web app, accessibility statements, privacy-preserving analytics and worker credential cards; and further trust guarantees, among them a package on financing referrals: licensed partners listed with their referral fees disclosed before any referral, never affecting ranking. Eleven more languages and fourteen more country packs are planned by an accepted decision. The reference hub in San Diego is decided and not deployed: Contribuda is its decided operator, today only a demo runs on synthetic data, and real sign-ups wait for a release review, counsel review and the project owner's recorded decision to open them. Its direction is already recorded: it is the exemplary hub where every new method lands first, and its ownership is to be transferred to a local operator through an open competition, on terms to be decided.

Some things in this book are not in the repository's designs at all, and the book says so rather than borrowing a status word for them. The house record that continues after completion, the owner's adviser as a role and each hub's defect observatory are directions of this book; so are the hub playbook for opening a hub as a Contribuda project and the synchronisation of a hub's organisation with that project. Contribuda's part in the international layer (cross-border deals and transactions, reputation across the mesh) is recorded as a principle, and its form is to be decided: it will be settled in a decision record that reconciles it with the hub exchange layer, where today each hub charges only its own participants.

## What there is not, said plainly

- **No production deployment.** Nothing serves real users anywhere; no hosted hub accepts sign-ups. The API refuses to start in production without its secrets and a secure origin, the container stack and the backup drill run in continuous integration on synthetic data, and no production backup target exists.
- **No provider connected.** No payment, e-mail, model, registry, storage or channel provider; every port has a fake. No model gateway is claimed Live, and the default application model is unavailable.
- **No real participant.** No real company, person, review or rating exists in the engine. No interviews with practitioners have taken place.
- **The civic engine is not yet designed.** Nothing in the repository designs it. Its decision record is to be written; it has no work package; the vote module, the public-works record and the institution's delivery record exist as sentences in this book and nowhere else.
- **The financing ring is not yet designed.** The repository's one financing item is the proposed package for listing licensed financing partners with disclosed referral fees. The build file, the inspector role, the stage closure, the disbursement instruction, the open statistics and the open standard have no work package.
- **Partners.** No lender, insurer, inspector, municipality, agency or civic organisation named anywhere in this book is connected. Naming an organisation records its public work; it implies no contact, interest or agreement.

> **Note.** How to read this chapter in a year
>
> When a thing lands, its sentence moves out of this chapter and into the chapters before it as plain description, and nothing else in the book changes. If this chapter grows instead of shrinking, something has gone wrong, and the book will say so.

> Live means tested. Deployed means used. We say which.
